title: Jefferson County CO well depth and cost
meta_description: In Jefferson County the median well depth is 228 ft and the median yield is 6 gpm. Drilling and completing a typical new well runs about $20,800-$34,800.
h1: What to expect from a water well in Jefferson County, Colorado
intro_html:
Jefferson County wells are a mixed bag. You have shallow alluvial spots along the valleys and some very deep holes in hard mountain rock from Evergreen and Conifer over toward the Front Range edge. County-wide the median total depth is 228 feet, but there are plenty of exceptions, from under 100 feet to over 600 feet and even deeper.

If you’re buying land or a home on a well here, you need to plan for fractured bedrock, variable yields, and a wide spread in drilling costs. The state records give us a good picture of what’s been drilled so far and what you’re likely to run into on your specific parcel.

sections.heading: How deep are wells in Jefferson County’s mountains
sections.html:
Across Jefferson County, the median well depth is 228 feet. The middle half of wells run from 54 to 431 feet, so you see everything from relatively shallow holes along drainages up to several hundred feet in the higher, harder rock. About 32% of wells are under 100 feet, 26% are 100–300 feet, 29% are 300–600 feet, and 14% go past 600 feet. The deepest on record hits 4,095 feet, which shows how stubborn the fractured bedrock can be.

In places like Evergreen, Conifer, and up toward the Clear Creek County line, it’s common to need more depth to find enough fractures. A driller’s bid will usually span a range, not a single number, because a lot depends on exactly how the granite and gneiss are cracked beneath your lot.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling here and how activity has changed
sections.html:
Jefferson County has 40,739 wells in the state records, with 24,748 marked as constructed and 25,536 reporting a total depth. Drilling really took off in the 1970s with 6,685 permits, stayed strong through the 1980s with 5,000, and peaked in the 1990s at 8,840 permits. Activity tapered after that: 5,216 in the 2000s, 2,854 in the 2010s, and 1,549 so far in the 2020s, with new permits still being issued through 2025.

The most active drillers on record are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 4,354 wells, James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.) with 2,123, and Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert) with 1,793. Around Evergreen, Lakewood, and up toward Gilpin County, many of the older homes are on these legacy wells, so looking up the original permit and completion report is worth your time.

sections.heading: Well yield in fractured bedrock: how much water you really get
sections.html:
Of the 9,118 wells that report a yield, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 9.5 gpm. That’s generally fine for a household well, especially with storage. About 4% of wells make under 1 gpm, 33% land in the 1–5 gpm range, 56% produce 5–15 gpm, and 8% show 15+ gpm.

Those low-yield wells matter: a few percent of dry or trickling holes can ruin a budget if you hit one. In the fractured-bedrock aquifer that underlies most of Jefferson County (37,133 wells), yield depends on intersecting enough fractures. About 34% of wells tie into the Denver Basin aquifers or are labeled that way, which can give more predictable long-term production but often at greater depth.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they say about the water table
sections.html:
Only 1,329 wells in Jefferson County report a static water level, but they give some guidance. The median depth to water is 75 feet, and the middle half run from 23 to 150 feet below the surface. That means plenty of wells have water relatively high in the hole, with others seeing deeper water in the higher, drier terrain.

By decade, median water levels have bounced around: around 26–30 feet in the 1950s–1960s, dropping to about 60 feet in the 1970s and 55 in the 1980s, then deeper at 120 feet in the 1990s. The 2000s show a shallow 18 feet, then 100 feet in the 2010s and 90 feet in the 2020s. That pattern is variable, not a clean up-or-down trend, so I treat it as site-specific rather than a simple declining water table story.

sections.heading: Drilling and completion costs in Jefferson County
sections.html:
Most of Jefferson County sits on fractured mountain bedrock (granite and gneiss), which is slow, hard drilling. Typical prices run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 228-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $14,800–$22,800 before you add pump, wiring, trenching, and pressure system.

All-in, a finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical generally runs about $20,800–$34,800 at that median depth. If you’re in higher terrain above Evergreen, Conifer, or along the Jefferson–Clear Creek County line, plan for the possibility of going deeper than the median and budget accordingly. Denver Basin-targeted wells that end up several hundred feet deeper will scale that cost straight up with footage.

sections.heading: Risks to watch: low yield, contamination, and septic layout
sections.html:
In addition to the 4% of wells under 1 gpm, Jefferson County has some environmental flags you should be aware of. Within roughly 10 miles, there are 327 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 244 historic mine features, and 91 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those don’t mean your specific well is contaminated, but they do justify water testing and a careful look at site history, especially near older mining areas.

Most permits are domestic or household use (70%), with some stock (3%), irrigation (1%), and a sizeable 20% for monitoring. When you lay out a new build in places like Evergreen, Brook Forest, or Kittredge, keep enough separation between well and septic, and leave room for future leach field repair. The steep mountain lots can make that tight.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot in Jefferson County
sections.html:
Before you close on a property, pull the state well permit and completion data. Jefferson County has 25,536 wells reporting depth and 9,118 reporting yield, so odds are good a nearby well tells you what to expect. In areas near Lakewood and Wheat Ridge, you may see more Denver Basin or alluvial influence; in the higher mountain terrain it’s mostly fractured bedrock.

If the lot doesn’t have a well yet, assume a depth somewhere within the 54–431 foot middle band, but be financially ready to go deeper. Plan on a household-only exempt well unless the water right says otherwise, and remember the 35 gpm pumping limit on exempt wells. Factor the $20,800–$34,800 well cost into your build budget right alongside driveway, power, and septic.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Jefferson County, Colorado?
faq.a: State records show a median well depth of 228 feet in Jefferson County. The middle half of wells are between 54 and 431 feet, with about 32% under 100 feet and 29% between 300 and 600 feet. Around 14% exceed 600 feet, and the single deepest well reaches 4,095 feet, reflecting the variable fractured-bedrock conditions across the county.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Jefferson County?
faq.a: Of the 9,118 wells that report yield in Jefferson County, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute. The middle half fall between 3.0 and 9.5 gpm. About 4% of wells produce under 1 gpm, 33% are in the 1–5 gpm range, 56% yield 5–15 gpm, and 8% exceed 15 gpm. For most household uses, 3–10 gpm with proper storage and plumbing works fine.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Jefferson County?
faq.a: In Jefferson County’s fractured granite and gneiss, drilling typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 228-foot median depth, the borehole alone is roughly $14,800–$22,800. Once you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished well commonly totals about $20,800–$34,800. Deeper wells, especially Denver Basin targets, will scale that cost up directly with extra footage.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Jefferson County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety varies by location and needs to be tested. Jefferson County has 327 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 244 historic mine features, and 91 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those regional numbers don’t mean your specific well is contaminated, but they are a strong reason to test for basic potability and, in some areas, metals and PFAS before relying on the water for drinking.

faq.q: Are wells drying up in Jefferson County or is the water table stable?
faq.a: The limited static water level data show a median of 75 feet, with the middle half between 23 and 150 feet below surface. By decade, median levels have swung from around 26–30 feet in the 1950s–1960s to 120 feet in the 1990s, 18 feet in the 2000s, and about 90–100 feet in the 2010s–2020s. That pattern is variable rather than a simple steady decline, so conditions are best evaluated site by site.
